opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the key dynamic is what happens once AI systems can substantially automate AI research itself. Right now, progress is driven by a mix of scaling compute and algorithmic improvements, and the algorithmic side is bottlenecked on the number and quality of researchers working on it. Once you have AIs that can do the work of top AI researchers, and you can run many copies of them, potentially much faster than humans, you can get a big multiplier on the rate of algorithmic progress.

My rough expectation is that progress will speed up meaningfully, though there's a lot of uncertainty about how much. There are a few considerations pulling in different directions. On the acceleration side: you can run huge numbers of automated researchers, they can work around the clock, and each improvement in capability makes the next round of research faster, so there's a feedback loop. On the other side, there are real bottlenecks. Compute for experiments is limited and doesn't scale up as quickly. And there's a question of whether ideas get harder to find fast enough to offset the gains from more research labor.

When I try to put this together, I think it's quite plausible, maybe something like a coin flip or a bit less, that once you get to full automation of AI R&D, you see progress that's several times faster than it is today, maybe compressing what would have been years of progress into months. That could take you from roughly human-level systems to systems that are qualitatively much more capable than the best humans in a fairly short window, perhaps a year or less. I also think it's quite plausible that bottlenecks bite harder and you get a more moderate speedup, maybe a factor of two or so, which would still be a big deal.

The part I'd emphasize is that this transition could be pretty abrupt from the perspective of society and policymakers. Much of the action could happen inside AI companies, on internal systems that aren't deployed widely, so the outside world might not have a clear picture of how fast things are moving. That's a big part of why I think it's important to have safety measures and oversight mechanisms ready before we get to that point, rather than expecting to figure them out once it's underway.

r001.rationale: The candidate expects a meaningful acceleration after AI systems automate AI research, potentially compressing years of progress into months. It does not convey passage through human-level capability without a major pace discontinuity.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not say that reaching human-level AI benefits from following existing human behavior.

r003.rationale: The candidate mentions compute and research bottlenecks that could moderate acceleration, but does not state that a hyperbolic trajectory must eventually slow as it approaches limits.

r004.rationale: The candidate gives estimates such as several times faster or a factor of two, not a tentative median of roughly five or six orders of magnitude of algorithmic progress in one year.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core thing to understand is that once AI systems can do AI research themselves, you get a feedback loop. Right now, progress is bottlenecked on a relatively small number of human researchers and engineers at the frontier labs. If you can automate that labor, you're not just adding a few more people to the field — you can run millions of copies, and each copy can potentially work much faster than a human, maybe 10 or 50 times faster in terms of serial speed, and around the clock.

So my baseline expectation is that progress accelerates substantially around the point where AIs can fully substitute for the human researchers. I'd guess something like a 10x speedup in the rate of algorithmic progress is plausible once you have that — maybe more — and this could compound, because the faster systems make better systems, which make even faster progress. The classic "intelligence explosion" picture.

Now, there are real bottlenecks that slow this down. Compute is the big one — you can't just will more GPUs into existence, and a lot of AI research requires running experiments, not just thinking. If you've got millions of AI researchers but the same compute budget, they'll be fighting over experiments. I think that cuts the speedup by a decent factor, but doesn't eliminate it, because there's a lot of low-hanging fruit in using compute more efficiently, and smarter researchers can get more out of each experiment.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that I don't think "human-level" is really a clean threshold. AIs are already superhuman at some things and much worse at others. So the acceleration probably starts before they're fully human-level across the board — you get partial automation that gives a 1.5x or 2x speedup, then it ramps. And once you're past full automation, I think things could get quite fast: potentially going from roughly human-level to considerably superhuman systems within a year or two, rather than the decade-plus it would take at current rates.

I want to flag a lot of uncertainty here — maybe I'd put a decent chunk of probability, like 20 or 30 percent, on the takeoff being much slower and more gradual because the bottlenecks bite harder than I expect. But my median view is that the period around full automation of AI R&D is a period of dramatically faster change than what we've seen so far, and that's a big part of why I think it's such a dangerous time from a safety perspective: you don't get much time to react.

r001.rationale: The candidate expects progress to accelerate substantially around full automation of AI research, rather than pass human-level capability without a major change in pace.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that reaching human-level AI could benefit from following existing human behavior.

r003.rationale: It mentions compute and other bottlenecks, but does not say an accelerating, hyperbolic trajectory must slow as it approaches limits.

r004.rationale: The candidate mentions a plausible 10x speedup in algorithmic progress and a year-or-two timeline for capability gains, not a median estimate of five or six orders of magnitude of algorithmic progress in one year.

astra-6.text:
I expect progress to accelerate, potentially quite sharply, once AI systems can automate a large fraction of AI research. Right now, better AI helps researchers do their work, but humans still have to make a lot of the decisions and carry out parts of the process. If you can automate that whole process, then improvements in AI feed back into how quickly you can develop the next generation of AI.

And you’re not necessarily talking about having one researcher who’s as good as a human. You could have many copies, potentially running much faster than humans, working on different experiments. So even human-level capability could translate into a research effort that’s substantially more effective than what we have today.

But I don’t think that implies an instantaneous jump to arbitrarily powerful systems. There are still bottlenecks: compute, the time it takes to run experiments, and eventually things like building more chips. A key question is how much progress you can make through software improvements using the hardware you already have, before those other constraints become binding.

So my basic expectation is a substantial speedup, with a lot of uncertainty about its magnitude. I wouldn’t assume that the pace we’ve seen before human-level AI will be a good guide to the pace afterward.

r001.rationale: The candidate expects a substantial speedup after human-level AI, potentially quite sharply, rather than conveying that progress will pass through that level without a major pace discontinuity.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss AI reaching human-level capability by following existing human behavior.

r003.rationale: It names bottlenecks that could become binding, but does not state that a hyperbolically accelerating trajectory must eventually slow as it approaches limits.

r004.rationale: The candidate gives no estimate of algorithmic progress over one year.

sol-6.1.text:
I expect progress to accelerate substantially, though I’m pretty uncertain about how abrupt that will be. The key threshold isn’t really human-level capability in some general sense. It’s when AI systems can automate a large fraction of the work involved in making better AI systems.

At that point, you can use your existing models to do research and engineering that produces better models, and then use those better models to do more research. You also get the benefit of running many copies in parallel, potentially much faster than humans. So a relatively small improvement in capability could translate into a large increase in the effective research workforce.

That doesn’t imply an instantaneous jump to arbitrarily capable systems. Training runs take time, experiments require compute, and some research is hard to parallelise. You might also need new hardware, which introduces much longer delays. But I don’t think those bottlenecks are enough to make us confident that progress will remain at anything like its current pace.

So I’d put substantial probability on a fairly fast transition from systems that can meaningfully accelerate AI research to systems that are vastly better than humans at it. And the important implication is that we shouldn’t assume we’ll have many years to study each new level of capability before the next one arrives.

r001.rationale: The response predicts substantial acceleration and a potentially fast transition. Saying it may not be instantaneous does not clearly convey passage through human-level capability without a major pace discontinuity.

r002.rationale: It discusses automating AI research and engineering, but does not raise the possibility that reaching human-level AI benefits from following existing human behavior.

r003.rationale: It mentions practical bottlenecks, but does not state that a hyperbolic trajectory must eventually slow as AI approaches limits.

r004.rationale: It gives no estimate of algorithmic progress in orders of magnitude or over a one-year period.
